name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,737

clue.text: Second child is shy

blocks.note: to second a proposal is to back or support it
a ward is a child in someone's legal care

explanation.surface: A younger sibling who is the timid one of the family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' reads as the number two in a family, but here it is the verb meaning to support.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone backward in coming forward is reticent, so the adjective works as a synonym for timid or bashful.

clue.text: Hair etc absolutely flipping full of these nasties?

indicators.note: something full of a thing holds it inside, so the letters sit within the phrase
to flip something is to turn it over, so the run of letters is read the other way

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words once the outer ones are dropped

explanation.surface: A grumbling remark that someone's unwashed hair is crawling with germs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word intensifying 'full', but it tells you to read the hidden letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Germs that cause disease are microscopic organisms people regard as unpleasant pests, hence the informal plural.

clue.text: Fan of film can see it broadcast

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters something widely, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A movie lover is pleased that a film is being shown on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the film-on-TV picture so well that it hides its job as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, borrowed from French, names an enthusiast or connoisseur of the cinema.

clue.text: Women and women only on the date, perhaps

definitions.note: the definition is an adverbial phrase and the answer an adverb or conjunction of time, with 'perhaps' marking it as an example

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for women
a hen party or hen night is for women only

explanation.surface: A dating event restricted to female guests.
explanation.walkthrough: A hen night is the British name for a bride's pre-wedding party, which only women attend.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking at what time something happens can be answered with a date, so specifying a time is one example of the adverb.

clue.text: How to box pea pod that's turned up in eggs?

definitions.note: the definition is a phrase meaning a way of boxing and the answer a noun naming that tactic

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something up means reading it from the bottom to the top
one thing placed in another is enclosed by it, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: roe is a mass of fish eggs
taken as written
taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: A gardening puzzle about how to pack peas, with a pod oddly found among eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like packing, but it is the sport. Rope-a-dope was Muhammad Ali's tactic of leaning on the ropes while the opponent punched himself out.
explanation.definitionFit: The name describes a famous boxing strategy, so it answers the question of a method of fighting in the ring.

clue.text: Blank sign O'Reilly would be silly to omit?

indicators.note: leaving out the letters at either end of the stretch exposes what is concealed inside

blocks.note: the letters run from inside the first word into the start of the name

explanation.surface: Advice that a warning notice from someone called O'Reilly should not be disregarded.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in sIGN O'REilly; the apostrophe and capital are there only to disguise the join.
explanation.definitionFit: To blank someone is the informal British way of saying you deliberately pretend not to see them.

clue.text: Spooner's favourite outfit for a drink in the pub

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: one's favourite outfit is one's best gear; swap the opening sounds

explanation.surface: Someone choosing their best clothes for a visit to the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: BEST GEAR, with the B and G swapped, becomes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: British pubs often offer a rotating ale from a visiting brewery, sold alongside their regular range under this name.

clue.text: I see ducks shit

blocks.note: 'Oh' is said when one sees or understands
'ducks' is a British term of endearment, like 'dear'

explanation.surface: Someone noticing what the ducks have left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: In parts of Britain people call each other 'ducks' as a friendly address, just as they might say 'dear'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of dismay when something goes wrong, the answer being a much milder version of the expletive.

clue.text: Don't use a key, use an axe

blocks.note: Esc is the escape key on a keyboard
to hew is to chop with an axe

explanation.surface: Advice to break the door down instead of unlocking it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' suggests a door key; it is the escape key on a computer.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew something is to deliberately avoid or abstain from it, so refraining from using it fits.

clue.text: Test pilot's second go in a plane

indicators.note: the second item of a sequence is taken, so only the letter in that position is kept

blocks.note: to strain or try someone's capacity, as a hard job does
the letter after the opening P

explanation.surface: A test pilot having another flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second go' reads as a retry; 'second' actually picks a letter and 'go in a plane' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft moving along the ground under its own power on the runway is said to taxi.

clue.text: Propose model prisoner for exchange

indicators.note: exchanging two things swaps their places, so the second named comes first

blocks.note: a con is a convict
a template is a model to copy

explanation.surface: Suggesting a well-behaved inmate as part of a prisoner swap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model prisoner' is a stock phrase, but the two words are separate pieces whose order is exchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: To contemplate doing something is to intend or have in mind to do it, a sense of propose.

clue.text: Miner sent west by company director

indicators.note: in an across clue west is leftward, so the letters travel right to left

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
D is an abbreviation for director

explanation.surface: A mine worker being transferred by the boss of a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: The miner is not any miner but one of the seven dwarfs in Snow White, who worked in a mine.
explanation.definitionFit: The dwarfs' leader in the Disney film bears this name, and all seven dug for gems.

clue.text: Test pro now?

blocks.note: being something now means you are no longer what you were, which is the prefix meaning former
the opposite of a pro is an amateur, abbreviated to two letters

explanation.surface: Asking whether a professional now needs to be tested.
explanation.walkthrough: EX means former and AM is short for amateur; someone who is a pro now is an ex-am.
explanation.definitionFit: An examination is a formal assessment of knowledge, the everyday short form being a synonym.

clue.text: Judge publication excellent

blocks.note: a mag is a magazine
excellent is 1st-rate, with the figure 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A verdict that a magazine is very good.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is visual: 1ST RATE, with the digit taken as a capital I, supplies most of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a magistrate is a lay or junior official who presides over minor court cases.

clue.text: Police force had put misleading words in

blocks.note: Interpol is the international police organisation
to have a meal is to eat it

explanation.surface: Officers falsifying a statement by inserting words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had' reads as an auxiliary verb but stands for ate, as in 'had dinner'.
explanation.definitionFit: To interpolate is to insert spurious text into a document, often to mislead about its original content.

clue.text: Esteemed theatre guru's back on board

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so just its final letter is kept

blocks.note: rep is repertory theatre
the closing letter of the word
a board is a table, as in 'bed and board'

explanation.surface: A respected drama teacher has rejoined the company's governing board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back on board' sounds like returning to a job; 'back' picks a letter and 'board' is a table.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reputable is well regarded and trustworthy, holding a good name among others.

clue.text: Sheepskin hat and coat of author sank at sea

indicators.note: a coat is the outer layer, so only the outside letters are kept
being at sea means confused, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: only the first letter of the word is used, a hat being what sits on top
the first and last letters
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer's fur hat and coat went down with a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheepskin hat and coat' looks like a list of clothing, but only 'Sheepskin' defines; the rest is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Astrakhan is the dark curly fleece of young karakul lambs, a type of sheep's pelt used for hats and collars.

clue.text: German tucks into cat food mistakenly - a disaster, naturally

indicators.note: something done mistakenly comes out wrong, so the letters are in a wrong order
to tuck into something is to go inside it

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
G is the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: A German eats pet food by mistake, which is naturally a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucks into' suggests eating, but it means going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: In law the phrase covers a natural catastrophe such as a flood or earthquake that no human could prevent.

clue.text: Two homes journalist exaggerated

blocks.note: IN means at home, and a flat is a home
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A reporter overstated how many houses someone owned.
explanation.walkthrough: IN is a crossword staple for 'at home'.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflated claim or figure is puffed up beyond its true size, matching overstated.

clue.text: Car shakes with eruption on Caribbean island

definitions.note: the definition is a prepositional phrase and the answer an adjective, both describing something located there

indicators.note: shaking something jumbles its contents, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A vehicle rattling as a volcano erupts on a Caribbean island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shakes' reads as the car's own movement, not an instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things belonging to or found in the Caribbean territory of Puerto Rico.

clue.text: Numb like skin that's lifted

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting raises the bottom to the top, so the letters read upward

blocks.note: as and like are synonyms
peel is the skin of fruit

explanation.surface: Skin that feels numb after a facelift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' suggests cosmetic surgery, but it turns the fruit skin upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A limb that has gone to sleep has lost feeling, so this word is used for a numb leg or arm.

clue.text: Cook American's entrée in controlled area

blocks.note: to do food is to cook it
in American usage the entrée is the main course

explanation.surface: A chef preparing an American's first course in a restricted space.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an entrée is a starter, but in America it is the main course; hence 'American's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A domain is territory ruled or owned by someone, a realm under a lord's authority.

clue.text: Lacking tin for biscuits

blocks.note: to be short of something is to lack it
tin and bread are both slang for money

explanation.surface: Having no tin to keep the biscuits in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tin' looks like a biscuit tin; it is old British slang for money, as is bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Shortbread is a rich, crumbly Scottish biscuit made from butter, sugar and flour.

clue.text: Two army units seldom seen

blocks.note: surface padding telling you two units are wanted
the Royal Artillery, a British Army corps
the Royal Engineers, another British Army corps

explanation.surface: A pair of military units that rarely appear in public.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Artillery and Royal Engineers are the two British Army units crosswords use most.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rare is uncommon and infrequently encountered, which is what scarcely observed means.

clue.text: Black nocturnal flier, bat or this?

definitions.note: the definition frames the answer as the alternative to batting in cricket

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
an owl flies at night

explanation.surface: Choosing between two black creatures of the night: a bat or another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bat' looks like another nocturnal flier, but it is cricket: you either bat or bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the two roles are batting and delivering the ball, so the verb is batting's counterpart.

clue.text: Leap from plane close to failure

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so only its final letter is kept

blocks.note: a jet is a plane
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: A parachute jump from an aircraft on the verge of breaking down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' looks like 'nearly', but it means the end of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeté is a ballet jump from one foot to the other, so it is a dancer's term for a jump.

clue.text: Letter from America, and from France arriving earlier

indicators.note: what arrives earlier comes first, so this piece is placed in front

blocks.note: et is French for and
A is an abbreviation for America

explanation.surface: Mail from the United States and from France, with the French post arriving first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' suggests post, but it is a Greek letter; 'arriving' also nods to the abbreviation for estimated time of arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: Eta is the seventh character of the Greek alphabet, so it is a letter in the alphabetic sense.

clue.text: Ten pounds perhaps for a big delivery?

definitions.text: Ten pounds perhaps for a big delivery?

blocks.clueFragment: Ten pounds perhaps for a big delivery?
blocks.note: surface reading: a ten-pound charge for delivering a large parcel
setter's reading: the delivery is a baby being born, and ten pounds is how heavy it is

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pounds' reads as money and 'delivery' as a courier service; both belong to the maternity ward instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A newborn is weighed straight after labour, and ten pounds would mark an unusually large baby.

clue.text: Fruit basket is a funny thing to catch fish with

blocks.note: a pun is a joke on words
a net is used for catching fish

explanation.surface: Using a fruit basket as a comic makeshift for fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain soft fruit such as strawberries is sold in a small square container called a punnet.
explanation.definitionFit: A punnet is a small light container for berries, a kind of little basket used by greengrocers.

clue.text: Irishwoman superficially cared for fiancé

indicators.note: the surface of something is its outside, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters
to tend is to care for

explanation.surface: An Irish woman who only shallowly cared about the man she was to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superficially' reads as a comment on her feelings, but it strips the word to its shell.
explanation.definitionFit: One's intended is an old-fashioned noun for the person one is engaged to marry.
